analysis.one_liner: Taxes insurers 50% of premium for selling substandard Medicare supplement (Medigap) policies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in March 1990, referred to two committees and several subcommittees, and it died in committee when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would standardize private 'Medigap' policies that seniors buy to fill Medicare's gaps. Insurers selling a policy that failed federal standards would owe a tax equal to half the premium. Standards covered benefits (minimum benefits plus optional extras), a uniform format for comparing policies, loss ratios (minimum 80% group / 70% individual), limits on preexisting-condition exclusions, guaranteed renewability, no medical underwriting, limits on first-year commissions (no more than 200% of renewal-year commissions), registration to block duplicate policies and sales to Medicaid beneficiaries, and an HHS advisory committee. It died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries buying Medigap: fewer confusing, overlapping, or duplicate policies; stronger loss ratios so more of each premium dollar actually pays claims; guaranteed renewability; limits on preexisting-condition exclusions; no medical underwriting; standardized benefit packages for easy comparison.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on the issuer of any Medigap policy that does not meet the federal standards [S2][S3].
Defines minimum benefits (hospital coinsurance, 365-day lifetime extension, blood deductibles, Part B coinsurance) plus a defined set of optional additional benefits [S3].
Requires a uniform format and language so consumers can compare policies [S3].
Sets loss ratios at 80% for group and 70% for individual policies, with annual filings and GAO audits [S3].
Restricts preexisting-condition exclusions, guarantees renewability, bars cancellation except for nonpayment or misrepresentation, and requires conversion rights when group coverage ends [S3].
Prohibits medical underwriting — issuance cannot be conditioned on health status [S3].
Caps first-year sales commissions at 200% of renewal-year commissions, curbing churning and replacement sales [S3].
Requires registration to block duplicate policies and sales to Medicaid beneficiaries, and creates an advisory committee including insurers, state regulators, and beneficiaries [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurers selling substandard Medigap policies, who would owe the 50% excise tax or incur compliance costs to meet the standards; agents facing commission caps.

drawbacks.text: A 50% excise tax on nonconforming policies is a severe penalty that could push some insurers out of the market, and compliance/registration requirements add costs that could show up in premiums [S3].
Standardization and benefit restrictions could reduce consumer choice among richer benefit designs; the 70% individual loss ratio leaves a wide margin over expected claims for many seniors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance strongly pro-consumer: clearer, standardized policies, higher loss ratios, guaranteed renewability, and curbs on churning outweigh the cost of some market consolidation and compliance burden, though the 50% excise tax is an unusually blunt enforcement tool.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to committee on March 12, 1990; referred to subcommittees with hearings in April and June 1990; never brought to a House vote before the Congress ended in January 1991 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Referred jointly to Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce on introduction day, then to Health and Environment and Commerce/Consumer Protection subcommittees [S1][S5].
Subcommittee and joint hearings were held in June 1990, but no markup or floor action followed [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and agents, who avoided the 50% excise tax, registration, loss-ratio, commission, and underwriting standards; Congress instead enacted a milder version later in 1990 (OBRA 1990), but as to this bill the industry escaped its provisions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and agents; seniors kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the single cosponsor was a Democrat, and the bill died in committee without floor action [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: Would face a 50% excise tax on substandard policies, plus standards on benefits, loss ratios, renewability, and commissions; insurers resisted rather than backed the bill.
First-year commissions capped at 200% of renewal commissions, discouraging churning and replacement sales.
